- When sentiment is consistently negative (avg < -0.4) over recent days, model tends to overcorrect downward; adjust forecast upward by 1-2% to avoid underestimating rebound.
- After a sharp price spike (e.g., >5% from prior peak), model often overshoots and fails to account for subsequent mean reversion; reduce forecast by 1-3% in next 3-5 days.
- If sentiment shifts from negative to positive mid-horizon, model frequently lags in recognizing the reversal; add 0.5-1.5% upward adjustment in the 5-7 day window following sentiment flip.
- Model underestimates true outcomes when sentiment is positive but recent price action is volatile or shows signs of “overbought” (e.g., 3 consecutive days > +3%); increase forecast by 1-2% to reflect momentum.
- In high volatility periods (e.g., >30% range over 5 days), model tends to smooth too much; allow 1-2% higher forecast variance to capture tail risk.
- When sentiment is neutral or mixed, model often defaults to historical mean; override with 1-2% upward bias if recent price action shows upward momentum or policy support.
- If true outcome exceeds forecast by >3% for 2+ consecutive days, model is likely underestimating supply/demand shock; increase forecast by 1-3% for next 3-5 days unless sentiment turns negative.
- Model tends to underestimate true outcomes when sentiment is positive but recent price action is flat or declining; add 0.5-1% upward bias to reflect potential “rebound trap” or policy-driven support.
